chunks: Al-Qasim and Fadalah narrated from Aban, from al-Hasan al-Sayqal, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Is an hour of contemplation better than standing [in prayer] for a night?' He replied, 'Yes.' And the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'An hour of contemplation is better than standing [in prayer] for a night.' I asked, 'How does one contemplate?' He said, 'One passes by ruins and dwellings, contemplates, and says: Where are your inhabitants? Where are those who built you? Why do you not respond!'

key_terms.قِيَامِ لَيْلَةٍ: Standing in prayer during the night

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual benefit of contemplating ruins in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: This hadith, recorded in *Kitab al-Zuhd*, highlights the Shia scholarly preference for deep, reflective contemplation (*tafakkur*) over mere ritualistic endurance, suggesting that intellectual engagement with the transient nature of the world yields greater spiritual fruit. The Imam illustrates this by directing the seeker to observe ruins (*khurabat*) and abandoned dwellings, using these physical remnants as catalysts for pondering mortality, the passage of time, and the ultimate return to the Creator. This practice aligns with the concept of *tadabbur* (reflection) as a means to purify the heart and strengthen faith through understanding the signs of God in creation.

en.shaykh-tahir-ridha-jaffer: 6.Al-Qāsim and Faḍālah [also] narrated from Abān, from al-Ḥasan alṢayqal who said,

“I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh (a), ‘Is an hour of contemplation better than standing vigil [in worship] at night?’ He replied, ‘Yes. The Messenger of Allah (ṣ) said that an hour of contemplation is better than standing for nightly-worship.’ I asked, ‘How should one contemplate?’ He said, ‘One should pass by ruins and [long abandoned] dwellings and [think to himself]saying, “Where are your inhabitants? Where are those who constructed you? Why do you not respond!?”’”
